description.en: The Asian Civilisations Museum is housed in the Empress Place Building, a neoclassical block completed as a courthouse in 1867 and later used by government offices; the name honours Queen Victoria as Empress of India. The museum explores links between Asian cultures, and its highlights include treasures from a ninth-century Tang dynasty shipwreck.

facts.text: The museum is housed in the former Empress Place Building. Major John F. A. McNair, the Colonial Engineer, designed it, and it was built between 1864 and 1867 for government offices. After independence it held the Immigration Department and the Registry of Births and Deaths. In 1907 the space in front was named Empress Place to remember Queen Victoria. The building was gazetted as a national monument in 1992.

sources.title: Former Empress Place Building (now Asian Civilisations Museum)

facts.text: The Asian Civilisations Museum first opened on 22 April 1997 in the Old Tao Nan School building on Armenian Street. It opened its main museum at Empress Place on 2 March 2003, after the building was restored. It was one of the early museums in the region to focus on cultures and civilisations from across the whole of Asia.

The Khoo Teck Puat Gallery holds cargo from the Tang Shipwreck, an Arab ship found in 1998 at a reef off Belitung Island in Indonesia. Its hull was made of timber planks sewn together, a method used for ships from the Persian Gulf. It carried more than 50,000 hand-painted bowls from Changsha in China, plus finer Chinese wares, including Yue celadon and white porcelain.

summary: An old iron footbridge across the Singapore River, built in 1869 and now a National Monument. Walk across it and look for the old sign that bans cattle and horses.

description.en: Built in 1869 and named after Governor William Cavenagh, this is one of the oldest bridges across the Singapore River; its ironwork was made in Glasgow and put together here. Today it is for pedestrians only, and an old sign at one end still forbids cattle and horses from crossing.

facts.text: The bridge was first proposed in 1867, the year the Straits Settlements became a Crown colony. It honours Sir Orfeur Cavenagh, the last governor of the Straits Settlements chosen by the East India Company; councillors picked his name over 'Edinburgh Bridge'. Its iron parts were made by P. & W. MacLellan in Glasgow, Scotland, and it was one of the last works built using Indian convict labour.

When Anderson Bridge was finished in 1910, motor traffic moved over to it, and Cavenagh Bridge was left mostly to people on foot and rickshaws. An old police sign on the bridge still forbids horses, cattle and any vehicle heavier than 3 hundredweight. Today it is a pedestrian bridge. On 15 October 2019 it became a National Monument, together with Anderson and Elgin Bridges, as the Singapore River Bridges.

summary: A tall memorial in War Memorial Park on Beach Road, built for the civilians who died during the Japanese Occupation of 1942 to 1945. Stop here to learn about a hard chapter of Singapore's past.

description.en: This memorial was unveiled on 15 February 1967, exactly 25 years after the fall of Singapore. Its four white concrete columns stand for the shared suffering of the Chinese, Malay, Indian and other communities, and are often called 'the chopsticks'. Remains of unidentified civilian victims lie beneath it, and a remembrance ceremony is held here every 15 February.
description.zh: 日本占领时期死难人民纪念碑于1967年2月15日揭幕，正值新加坡沦陷25周年。四根白色混凝土立柱代表华族、马来族、印度族和其他族群共同承受的苦难，被人们称为“筷子”。碑下安葬着战后寻获的无名遇难者遗骸，每年2月15日都在这里举行追思仪式。

source.publisher: EARTH ONLINE (Wsamme); map data © OpenStreetMap contributors

facts.text: In 1962, building work in Singapore uncovered mass graves, including more than 40 at Siglap, in an area later called the 'Valley of Death'. The dead were victims of Sook Ching, an operation during the Japanese Occupation in which mainly Chinese men were arrested and killed. The Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce set up a fund for a memorial in 1963. Today the remains rest in 606 urns in a vault under the monument.

The memorial was designed by the firm Swan & Maclaren. Its four tapering columns stand for the Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasian communities, and many people call them the 'Four Chopsticks'. Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew unveiled it on 15 February 1967, the 25th anniversary of the British surrender. A memorial service for people of different faiths is held here every 15 February, which is also Total Defence Day.

description.en: Bay South garden opened in 2012 on reclaimed land at Marina Bay. Its 18 Supertrees, 25 to 50 metres tall and covered in plants, collect rainwater and some carry solar panels, and they light up for a nightly light-and-sound show. The Flower Dome is one of the largest glass greenhouses in the world, and the Cloud Forest wraps a 35-metre misty mountain with an indoor waterfall.

facts.text: The park was part of a national plan to move Singapore from a 'Garden City' to a 'City in a Garden'. A design competition in 2006 drew more than 70 entries from 170 firms in 24 countries. It is made up of three gardens: Bay South, the biggest at 54 hectares, Bay East and Bay Central. Bay South opened to the public on 29 June 2012.

The 18 Supertrees are vertical gardens between 25 and 50 metres tall. Besides holding plants and giving shade, they gather solar energy and rainwater and help vent and cool the conservatories. The two conservatories, designed by WilkinsonEyre, are the Flower Dome, about 1.2 hectares, and the Cloud Forest, about 0.8 hectares, which has a 35-metre waterfall inside. Guinness World Records listed the Flower Dome as the largest glass greenhouse in its 2015 book.

facts.text: The bridge is a 280-metre walkway joining Marina Centre and Marina South. Its steel frame twists like the double helix of DNA, but it turns to the left, the opposite way to real DNA. At night, pairs of letters lit in red and green appear along it: c and g, a and t. They stand for cytosine, guanine, adenine and thymine, the four bases of DNA.

Architects from the COX Group in Australia and Architects 61 in Singapore designed the bridge, with engineering by Arup. About 650 tonnes of duplex stainless steel went into it. Building started in 2007, half of it opened on 24 April 2010, and the whole bridge opened on 18 July 2010, completing the walking loop around Marina Bay. It has four viewing platforms that look out over the bay.

It stores water, protects low-lying areas from floods and keeps the water level steady. Its grassy green roof is a popular spot for kite-flying and picnics.
description.zh: 滨海堤坝于2008年落成，横跨滨海水道出海口，把海湾变成了位于市中心的淡水水库。它兼具蓄水、防洪和稳定水位三项功能，大雨又逢涨潮时可开闸或抽水排入大海。绿草如茵的屋顶是市民放风筝和野餐的好去处。

source.title: EARTH ONLINE · City Brush Singapore dataset (landmark placement and intro card)
source.publisher: EARTH ONLINE (Wsamme); map data © OpenStreetMap contributors

facts.text: The barrage closes off the 350-metre-wide Marina Channel and does three jobs. It holds back the sea, so rain collects into a freshwater reservoir. It guards low areas such as Chinatown, Boat Quay, Jalan Besar and Geylang from floods: at low tide, nine crest gates let storm water run out to sea, and at high tide, big pumps push it out. Its steady water level also suits kayaking, sailing and dragon boating.

Lee Kuan Yew first suggested damming Marina Channel in 1987, as a way to make Singapore less dependent on outside water. The barrage officially opened on 31 October 2008. From April 2009, rain slowly replaced the salt water in the basin, and on 20 November 2010 Lee commissioned it as a freshwater reservoir. It was Singapore's 15th reservoir and the first in the city centre, with a 10,000-hectare catchment.

description.en: The Merlion is Singapore's best-known symbol: the lion's head recalls the old name Singapura, the 'lion city', and the fish body its beginnings as a fishing village. The 8.6-metre statue by Lim Nang Seng was unveiled in 1972 and moved to this spot in 2002, where it spouts water into Marina Bay.

facts.text: The Merlion began in 1964 as a logo, not a statue. Alec Fraser-Brunner, a British zoologist who was then curator of the Van Kleef Aquarium, drew it for the Singapore Tourist Promotion Board. The fish body is a reminder of Temasek, the early fishing village here. The lion head points to the Malay Annals story of Sang Nila Utama, the prince who named the island Singapura.

sources.title: Celebrating 50 Years of the Merlion: Stories Behind the National Icon

facts.text: Sculptor Lim Nang Seng made the first statue from a design by the artist Kwan Sai Kheong, and his eight children helped him. Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew unveiled it at the mouth of the Singapore River on 15 September 1972. The main figure stands 8.6 metres tall, and a smaller 'Merlion cub' of 2 metres stands nearby. The statue faces east, a direction seen as lucky in feng shui.

sources.title: Celebrating 50 Years of the Merlion: Stories Behind the National Icon

facts.text: Once the Esplanade Bridge was finished in 1997, people on the waterfront could no longer see the Merlion clearly. So in April 2002 the 70-tonne statue was lifted by crane, carried by barge and set on a new pier beside The Fullerton Hotel, about 120 metres from where it first stood. In February 2009 lightning struck it, knocking off a piece of its mane, and it was closed for repairs.

facts.text: The building is named after Robert Fullerton, the first Governor of the Straits Settlements, and its northern end sits where Fort Fullerton once stood. Work began in February 1924 and ended in June 1928. The design came from Major P.H. Keys of Keys & Dowdeswell, a Shanghai firm that won a design competition. Look for its two-storey rows of fluted Doric columns and the portico over the main entrance.

The General Post Office filled the lower floors, while the Singapore Club and the Exchange were among the other tenants. In the last days before the British surrender in 1942, the building was used as a hospital, and later it became the base of the Japanese military administration. The post office moved out in March 1996. The building reopened as a hotel on 1 January 2001 and became a National Monument in December 2015.

summary: A working mosque on South Bridge Road in Chinatown, built in the 1830s by Tamil Muslim traders. Come to see its South Indian gateway and twin minarets, and remember to dress modestly.

description.en: Masjid Jamae was founded around 1826 by Chulia Muslims from the Coromandel Coast of southern India, and the present building went up between 1830 and 1835, making it one of Singapore's oldest mosques. The twin towers beside the gate, with their stacked, shrinking tiers, mix South Indian and neoclassical styles.
description.zh: 詹美回教堂由来自南印度科罗曼德海岸的朱利亚穆斯林于1826年前后创建，现今的建筑在1830至1835年间建成，是新加坡最古老的清真寺之一。正门两侧的塔楼一层层向上收小，融合了南印度与新古典主义等多种风格。

source.title: EARTH ONLINE · City Brush Singapore dataset (landmark placement and intro card)
source.publisher: EARTH ONLINE (Wsamme); map data © OpenStreetMap contributors

facts.text: The mosque was started around 1826 by the Chulia community, Tamil Muslim merchants who were led by a pioneer named Anser Sahib. Their first mosque on this site was a simple wooden building. Between 1830 and 1835 it was replaced by the brick and plaster building that still stands on South Bridge Road today. It was gazetted as a National Monument on 19 November 1974.

The building mixes several styles. Its entrance gateway, framed by two tall minarets, follows South Indian designs, while the prayer halls show Neoclassical features such as Tuscan columns and pilasters. Chinese touches can also be found in the building. The mosque is one of the few in Singapore that offers religious classes in Tamil, and it has room for about 1,500 worshippers.

Over time the mosque took on a wider role in the community. In 1894 the Nagore Dargah, a shrine on the neighbouring street, was placed under the same trustees. In 1917 the mosque became a waqf, which means it is held in trust for the Muslim community, and in 1968 it came under MUIS, the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore.

accessNotes.text: Non-Muslim visitors are welcome. Wear modest clothing; robes are lent free at the entrance, and group visits are by appointment.

summary: A busy hawker centre in Chinatown, set in a market building that dates from the late 1920s. Come for a simple sit-down meal and to see how an old wet market became a food centre.

facts.text: The land under Maxwell Food Centre was once a Chinese burial ground, cleared in 1907. Work on a municipal market began here in 1927. At first it sold mainly fresh produce, but many hawkers kept trading on the streets outside, so stallholders found business hard. Cooked food stalls and tables were added in 1930, an early sign of what the place would later become.

After the Second World War, a government 'Family Restaurant' selling cheap meals opened here, the first of a chain started in 1946. In 1972, produce sellers from Telok Ayer Market moved in. Later, about 70 cooked-food hawkers who had worked in back lanes around China Square were moved here, and in 1987 the market officially became a food centre. Its present name came with an upgrade finished in 2001.

description.en: Built in 1934, the Old Hill Street Police Station once held a police station and quarters for officers and their families. More than 900 window shutters are painted in rainbow colours, making it one of the most photographed buildings by the Singapore River. It became a National Monument in 1998 and now houses government ministries.

source.publisher: EARTH ONLINE (Wsamme); map data © OpenStreetMap contributors

facts.text: Built between 1931 and 1934, the building was designed in a Neoclassical style by Frank D. Ward, chief architect of the Public Works Department. It was much more than a police station. The upper floors held homes for 180 single men and 140 married constables, plus quarters for their inspectors, while the ground floor had the station itself, garages and a parade square.

The building's colours have changed over the years. In 1943, during the war, the Japanese painted it brown as camouflage, and it was repainted white in 1949. The police had moved out by December 1980, and government offices took over. It became a National Monument on 18 December 1998, and in a renovation the next year its more than 900 windows were painted in rainbow colours.

summary: Two car-free streets in the heart of Chinatown, lined with restored shophouses and small shops. Walk them to see old shophouse fronts and learn how early Chinese migrants lived here.

facts.text: Pagoda Street is named after the tower-like gateway, or gopuram, of the Sri Mariamman Temple nearby. In the early 1900s many of its shophouses became lodging houses for coolies, or hired labourers, and these closed after the coolie trade ended in the 1930s. The street was also known for opium smoking. Today the Chinatown Heritage Centre here shows the lives of early Chinese settlers.

Trengganu Street takes its name from Terengganu, a state on the Malay Peninsula. In Chinese it was known as the cross street of Kreta Ayer, and it was once called the Piccadilly of Chinese Singapore. Like Pagoda Street, it is now a pedestrian mall with shops on both sides, and both streets have shophouses in the painted-lady style.

facts.text: The building on Armenian Street was once a wing of the Asian Civilisations Museum. That wing closed on 1 January 2006 for a large revamp, and planners chose a Peranakan theme over other ideas, such as a children's museum. The Peranakan Museum opened on 25 April 2008 with ten permanent galleries. It closed for renovation in April 2019 and reopened on 17 February 2023.

The original ten galleries followed Peranakan life from beginning to end. They started with the origins of different Peranakan communities, then gave several rooms to the traditional wedding and its ceremonies. Other rooms showed nonya crafts such as beadwork, religious life, the public lives of well-known Peranakans, and food and feasting. A key object is a wedding bed that once belonged to a woman in Penang.

description.en: Founded in 1827 by the merchant Naraina Pillai, Sri Mariamman is Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, dedicated to the goddess Mariamman, known for curing illness. Its tall entrance tower is covered with brightly painted deities, and every year devotees walk barefoot over hot coals during the Theemithi festival.

facts.text: The temple was started by Naraina Pillai, a Penang man working as a government clerk, who came to Singapore with Stamford Raffles in 1819. He was granted the South Bridge Road site in 1823, and a simple wood-and-attap temple stood there by 1827. The oldest parts of today's brick temple date from around 1843, and the gopuram was rebuilt in 1925. It became a National Monument in 1973.

About a week before Deepavali each year, the temple holds the Theemithi festival in honour of the goddess Draupadi. Devotees walk in procession for about four kilometres from Sri Srinivasa Perumal Temple on Serangoon Road. At the temple, male devotees cross roughly three metres of burning charcoal barefoot, then step into a pit of milk. Visitors on any day leave their shoes near the entrance, as footwear is not worn inside.

description.en: Built between 1839 and 1842, Thian Hock Keng is one of Singapore's oldest and most important Hokkien temples, dedicated to Mazu, goddess of the sea. It once stood on the shoreline, and newly arrived immigrants came here to give thanks for a safe voyage. It was built with traditional methods, reportedly without nails, and became a National Monument in 1973.

facts.text: Work on the temple began in 1839 and ended in 1842. At that time it stood on the shoreline of Telok Ayer Basin, before land reclamation in the 1880s moved the sea further away. New arrivals from China came here to thank Mazu, goddess of the sea, for bringing them safely across. The Hokkien Huay Kuan clan association was set up inside its grounds in 1840.

The temple is built in the traditional Hokkien style. All of its building materials came from China, and craftsmen from Fujian made the carvings and decorations. It was gazetted as a national monument on 6 July 1973. After a major restoration from 1998 to 2000, it received an honourable mention in the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards in 2001.

facts.text: Hajjah Fatimah was a wealthy businesswoman who ran the trading business of her husband, a Bugis prince and merchant, after his death. When thieves broke into her house and it was later set on fire, she gave the land and money for a mosque on the same site, on Java Road. It was finished in 1846, and it was the first local mosque named after a woman.

The building mixes ideas from different traditions. A golden dome sits over the prayer hall, and the windows have pointed arches in a Gothic style. The eight-sided minaret looks like the steeple of the first St Andrew's Church, and because it started to tilt after it was built, people called it the 'Leaning Tower of Singapore'. Hajjah Fatimah is buried in a mausoleum at the mosque.

facts.text: Four Armenian brothers, the Sarkies, opened the hotel on 1 December 1887 with just ten rooms. It started in a beach bungalow they leased from its owner, Syed Mohamed Alsagoff. That house had earlier been Emmerson's Hotel and then a boarding house for Raffles Institution boys. The main building you see today replaced the bungalow in 1899. It was designed by Regent Alfred John Bidwell of the firm Swan & Maclaren.

The Singapore Sling cocktail was first mixed at the hotel's Long Bar by a barman named Ngiam Tong Boon. During the Japanese Occupation the hotel was given a new name, Syonan Ryokan, meaning an inn of occupied Singapore. It was made a National Monument on 4 March 1987. Since then it has closed twice for long restorations, from 1989 to 1991 and again from December 2017 to August 2019.

facts.text: The first mosque here grew out of an agreement between Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor and the British East India Company, which set land aside for a royal mosque. Stamford Raffles pledged 3,000 Spanish dollars from the Company towards building it. That first mosque was a one-storey brick building with a two-tier pitched roof, and by the 1920s it was about a hundred years old.

Today's mosque was finished in 1932. Irish architect Denis Santry of the firm Swan & Maclaren designed it in the Indo-Saracenic style, which mixes Indian and Islamic forms with European features. Look at the base of each dome: a band of glass bottle ends, collected and given by poor people, runs around it. The mosque became a National Monument in 1975.

name: Little India

source.title: Little India, Singapore

summary: A conservation district of shophouses, temples and shops around Serangoon Road, with deep South Asian roots. Walk its streets to see places of worship of many faiths, especially at festival times such as Deepavali.

facts.text: The area began as a place where Europeans traded cattle. The Serangoon River nearby made it good land for raising animals, and Indian migrants found work there looking after livestock. When the swamps were drained, the European traders moved away, but many of the workers stayed, and the district became mainly South Asian. Locally it is also called Tekka, a name kept by Tekka Centre.

Many faiths have places of worship close together here. Within the district are Hindu temples such as Sri Srinivasa Perumal, Chinese temples such as Leong San See and Sakya Muni Buddha Gaya, mosques such as Masjid Abdul Gaffoor, and Kampong Kapor Methodist Church. Little India was gazetted as a conservation area on 7 July 1989, and more buildings nearby were conserved in later decades.

facts.text: The Gardens were started on this site in 1859 by an Agri-Horticultural Society, which designed them in the English Landscape style. Swan Lake was dug out in 1866. In July 2015 the Gardens were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. They were the first tropical botanic garden on the list, and only the third botanic garden of any kind to be added.

sources.title: The History of Singapore Botanic Gardens

facts.text: Henry Ridley, known as 'Mad Ridley', became director of the Gardens in 1888. The Gardens introduced, tested and promoted Para rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) as a crop, and in the early 20th century rubber brought great wealth to Southeast Asia. Malaya later led the whole world in growing and selling natural rubber abroad.

sources.title: The History of Singapore Botanic Gardens

facts.text: A patch of tropical rainforest, about six hectares in size, grows inside the Gardens, and it was already here before the Gardens were laid out. Orchids have a long history here too: the Gardens began breeding new orchid hybrids in 1928. Today the National Orchid Garden is the biggest draw for visitors to the Botanic Gardens, so leave some time for it.

name: Adam Road Food Centre

source.title: Adam Road Food Centre

summary: A hawker centre beside the Bukit Timah Canal, open since 1974 and long known for Malay food. Stop for a simple meal under old shady trees while travelling through Bukit Timah.

facts.text: In 1971, temporary food stalls were set up in sheds beside the Bukit Timah Canal, across the road from today's site. When a road project affected that spot, the hawkers moved across, and the new centre opened on 28 September 1974 with 32 cooked-food stalls. It was part of a 1970s government effort to move hawkers off the streets and into food centres.

Because it sits close to the canal, the centre often flooded after heavy rain in the 1980s. A five-month upgrade costing S$1.73 million was finished in 2002. It raised the floor, lifted the roof and added an outdoor courtyard, but it kept the nine-sided shape and five old angsana trees, which give shade and soften the sound of traffic.

From its early years, the centre was known for Malay dishes such as nasi lemak and mutton soup. In the 1980s it was the set lunch place for police officers after their shifts, and it also drew university students, drivers and people living nearby. In 2007 the National Heritage Board added it to the Bukit Timah Heritage Trail.

name: Bukit Timah Nature Reserve

source.title: Bukit Timah Nature Reserve

summary: A protected rainforest around Bukit Timah Hill, the highest natural peak in Singapore. Come for forest trails, a walk up to the summit and a chance to spot wildlife close to the city.

facts.text: In 1882, Nathaniel Cantley, head of the Singapore Botanic Gardens, was asked to study the forests of the Straits Settlements. His advice led to Bukit Timah becoming a forest reserve in 1883. While many other reserves were later cut for timber, this one was kept, and the Nature Reserves Ordinance of 1951 gave it formal protection. It was declared an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2011.

The reserve covers only about two square kilometres, yet it holds more than 840 kinds of flowering plants and more than 500 kinds of animals. The hill rises to about 165 metres. It was once quarried for granite, but quarrying stopped in the mid-1900s. In late 2013, the Eco-Link@BKE, a bridge built for wildlife, was completed over the nearby expressway.

In 1940, there were also plans to turn garages behind the Seng Poh Road flats into bomb shelters.

name: Fort Siloso

source.title: Fort Siloso

summary: A restored British coastal fort on Sentosa, with tunnels, bunkers and gun positions. Go to see how the island guarded Singapore's harbour, and to learn what happened here in the Second World War.

facts.text: The British built Fort Siloso to protect Keppel Harbour, after a Royal Engineers officer reported that the harbour needed defending. Workers blew the top off Mount Siloso to make flat platforms for the guns. The weapons were upgraded many times: 7-inch and 64-pounder guns by the 1880s, five 10-inch guns in the 1890s, then searchlights and anti-aircraft machine guns in the 1930s.

The guns were placed to meet an attack from the sea to the south. In February 1942, when Japanese forces came from the north instead, the gunners turned them around to fire inland. During the Japanese Occupation, from 1942 to 1945, the fort was used as a prisoner-of-war camp. On 15 February 2022 it was gazetted as one of Singapore's National Monuments.

name: MacRitchie Reservoir Park

source.title: Bandstand and Zig-Zag Bridge at MacRitchie Reservoir

summary: Singapore's first reservoir, surrounded by forest trails at the edge of a large nature reserve. Hike to the TreeTop Walk for a view over the forest, or stroll by the water.

facts.text: MacRitchie was Singapore's first reservoir. It was made in the 1860s by holding back water behind an earth embankment, and it was first called the Impounding Reservoir. It became Thomson Road Reservoir in 1907 and was given its present name in 1922, after Municipal Engineer James MacRitchie. The park's bandstand and zig-zag bridge were given conservation status in 2009.

sources.title: Bandstand and Zig-Zag Bridge at MacRitchie Reservoir

facts.text: The TreeTop Walk is a 250-metre free-standing suspension bridge between Bukit Peirce and Bukit Kalang, the two highest points in the MacRitchie forest. At its highest point it is 25 metres up, which gives you a view across the top of the trees. The bridge was finished in July 2004 and officially opened on 5 November 2004.

The reservoir sits at the south-eastern end of the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, Singapore's largest nature reserve. Look out for the Raffles' Banded Langur, which is critically endangered in Singapore, as well as the Lesser Mousedeer and the Clouded Monitor Lizard. Pets are not allowed in the reserve, fishing is not allowed, and visitors should keep to the marked trails.

Some follow Peranakan styles, while others mix Chinese and other decorative styles, and the government protected them for conservation in 1991. The road was called Lorong E East Coast until 1934, when it was renamed after the businessman Cheong Koon Seng. It stayed a Peranakan enclave until the 1970s.

The wider Joo Chiat district takes its name from Chew Joo Chiat (1857-1926), who was known as the "King of Katong". Before the houses came, much of the area was coconut and cotton plantations, with a few villages and seaside bungalows. Peranakan families later settled in Joo Chiat and built many of the shophouses that are now conserved.

summary: A long, quiet seaside park on the north-east tip of Singapore, looking across to Pulau Ubin. Come for beach walks, sea breezes and picnics, and to remember a painful wartime event.

facts.text: This shore saw killings during the Japanese occupation. On 20 February 1942, as part of the Sook Ching operation, Japanese military police shot 66 Chinese men on the beach here. A National Heritage Board plaque in the park remembers them. The plaque also notes that nearby Tanah Merah Besar Beach, which now lies under the airport runway, was another site of killings. facts.text: In the 1600s this coast was called Tanjung Rusa. By the 1800s it had become Tanjung Changi, possibly named after a plant that once grew widely here. Today the park covers 28 hectares and stretches about 3.3 km. Today many people still come for picnics, fishing and jogging, and to watch planes coming in to land.

name: Pulau Ubin

source.title: Pulau Ubin

summary: A quiet island off Singapore's north-east coast with old granite quarries, kampung village houses and the Chek Jawa wetlands. Walk or cycle around it at an easy pace.

facts.text: The island's old Malay name, Pulau Batu Jubin, means "Granite Stone Island". Granite cut here was used for the Causeway, the Istana and Horsburgh Lighthouse, and for early public housing and roads in the 1970s. The last working quarry, Ketam Quarry, closed in May 1999. Many old pits have since filled with rainwater and now give homes to plants and animals.

Chek Jawa is a wetland of about 100 hectares at the south-eastern tip of the island. Plans to reclaim its land were approved in 1992, but public attention in 2001 led the government to put the work off. Today a boardwalk runs through its mangrove, and the shore is home to sea hares, octopuses, starfish and nudibranchs.

source.title: Kranji Marshes

summary: A freshwater marsh and woodland park beside Kranji Reservoir in the north of Singapore. Bring binoculars and come to look for wetland birds in a quiet, open landscape.

facts.text: The marsh formed after the Kranji River was dammed to create Kranji Reservoir. In 1990 the Nature Society (Singapore) wrote a proposal showing why the area was worth protecting, and the idea was taken into the government's Singapore Green Plan of 1993. In 2005 the area was made a park and named Kranji Marshes Park. It opened to the public on 1 February 2016.

The park covers 54 hectares of wetland and woodland. It is home to a number of endangered birds, and at least 170 bird species have been recorded here. In 2008 the Nature Society (Singapore) adopted this stretch of wetland and, with help from sponsors, ran a restoration programme together with PUB and the National Parks Board (NParks).

summary: A Commonwealth war cemetery and memorial in the north of Singapore. Visit to learn about the Second World War in Singapore and Malaya, and to remember the people who died in it.

description.en: Unveiled in 1957, the Kranji War Memorial honours Allied servicemen who died defending Singapore and Malaya in the Second World War. More than 4,000 graves line the slope, and the walls carry over 24,000 names of those with no known grave. Its columns stand for the army, the wing-shaped roof for the air force and the periscope-like top for the navy.
description.zh: 克兰芝战争纪念碑于1957年揭幕，纪念二战中为保卫新加坡和马来亚而牺牲的盟军将士。山坡上排列着四千多座墓碑，纪念墙上刻着两万四千多名下落不明者的名字。立柱代表陆军，机翼般的屋顶代表空军，顶端形似潜望镜，代表海军。

source.title: EARTH ONLINE · City Brush Singapore dataset (landmark placement and intro card)
source.publisher: EARTH ONLINE (Wsamme); map data © OpenStreetMap contributors

facts.text: The memorial is shaped to stand for the three armed services. Its columns represent the army, a roof shaped like a wing represents the air force, and the top recalls the tower of a submarine for the navy. More than 24,000 Allied soldiers, sailors and airmen who have no known grave are named on its columns. Colin St Clair Oakes designed both the memorial and the cemetery.

During the Japanese Occupation there was a prisoner-of-war camp at Kranji and a hospital nearby, and many who died there were buried on this ground. In 1946 the site was chosen as Singapore's war cemetery, and graves from Changi, Buona Vista and other places were moved here. It now holds more than 4,400 graves, over 800 of them unidentified. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission looks after it.

Next to the war graves is the State Cemetery, where Singapore's first two presidents, Yusof bin Ishak and Benjamin Henry Sheares, are buried. The site also has graves from later conflicts, including the Malayan Emergency and Konfrontasi, as well as burials from the First World War. The memorial's inscription ends with the words 'They died for all free men'.

name: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve

source.title: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve

summary: A wetland nature reserve in northern Singapore, with mangroves, mudflats, ponds and forest. Walk its trails to look for migratory shorebirds and other wetland wildlife.

facts.text: In 1989 part of this area became a nature park, and the park was opened officially on 6 December 1993 by Goh Chok Tong, who was Prime Minister at the time. In 2002 it was gazetted as a 130-hectare nature reserve, and in 2003 it was named Singapore's first ASEAN Heritage Park. It has since expanded to about 202 hectares of mangrove, mudflat, pond and forest.

sources.title: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve: Special Features

facts.text: The reserve sits on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, a huge bird migration route that runs from the Russian Far East and Alaska down to Australia and New Zealand. It formally joined the flyway's network of sites in 2002. Shorebirds such as the common redshank, common greenshank and whimbrel use the reserve for more than half of each year. Saltwater crocodiles also turn up now and then.

facts.text: The building first opened as the Kreta Ayer Complex and was renamed Chinatown Complex in 1984. It was built to give street hawkers from Smith, Trengganu, Pagoda and Temple Streets a permanent home, and about 300 of them moved in. After an upgrade, it reopened in 2008 with more than 700 stalls.
